# Disciplines {#sec-chapter-disciplines}

```{=typst}
#label("sec-chapter-disciplines")

// Rationale: Chapter opener at 80% width: a shepherd tending magical creatures in a peaceful glade, representing the discipline of care and guidance.
#image("assets/images/placeholder-ch08-disciplines.png", width: 80%)

_Figure 10.1: Disciplines_

#pagebreak()

Disciplines are the signature mechanic of _Heroes of Legend._ They're how the game knows what your hero has mastered. Not just skills, _domains of power._ Fire. Melee. Protection. The forces and forms your character has attuned to through training, study, or sheer stubborn repetition.

Here's the important part: *Disciplines are prerequisites, not rolls.* You don't roll your Fire Discipline. You don't add your Melee Discipline to an attack. Disciplines are the gate, you need them to _unlock_ abilities and spells. Skills are exempt, they have no Discipline prerequisites at all (@sec-chapter-skills) Once you've got them, they represent permanent mastery. No expiration. No forgetting.

#pagebreak()

== What Are Disciplines?

A Discipline represents a domain of expertise or power your hero has internalized. It's the difference between "I picked up a sword once" and "I've trained with blades for ten years." Between "I read a book about fire" and "Fire answers when I call."

*Example:* A warrior with 3 ranks in Melee has spent years mastering swords, every angle, every grip, every weakness in every guard. A mage with 3 ranks in Fire doesn't just cast flames, they _understand_ flame, the way a shipwright understands wood. A ranger with 2 ranks in Animal has bonded with the wild in ways city-folk will never comprehend.

You _collect_ them. They're permanent markers on your character sheet that say: "I've earned this."

#pagebreak()

Twenty-three Disciplines. Nine categories. Your hero's path through them defines everything they can do.

#pagebreak()

== Acquiring Disciplines

=== Starting Disciplines

Your starting Disciplines come from your ancestry (1), your culture (2, or 1 for free-choice cultures), and your class (see the Class Disciplines table below).

=== Class Disciplines

Your class hands you specific Disciplines at creation. These are your foundation, what your training, tradition, or sheer talent has already taught you:

#figure(
  align(center)[#table(
    columns: (25%, 75%),
    align: (auto, auto,),
    table.header([Class], [Starting Disciplines],),
    [Protector], [1 Armor + 1 Shields],
    [Blade], [1 Melee + 1 Stealth],
    [Arcanist], [1 Fire + 1 Energy],
    [Shepherd], [1 Shields + 1 Animal],
    [Intellect], [1 Lore + 1 any],
    [Odd], [2 of any type, different categories],
    [Leader], [1 Tactics + 1 Shields],
    [Unbalanced], [1 Fire + 1 Water (or Earth/Wind)],
    [Shadow], [1 Stealth + 1 Sleight],
  )],
  kind: table,
  numbering: none,
  outlined: false,
)

Starting Disciplines from ancestry, culture, and class are always rank 1. When two fixed grants hand you the same Discipline, the second is explicit waste: no rank up, no extra Development Points, just a reminder of where you came from. Gorma the dwarf takes Melee from her bloodline and Melee again from her mountain, and she is still rank 1. You may not spend both discretionary picks on the same Discipline to start with rank 2. You may deepen a Discipline you already have to rank 2 (2 same) with Background DP at creation, per @sec-chapter-character-creation Depth beyond rank 2 comes from progression picks at levels 3, 6, and 9.

=== Progression

At levels 3, 6, and 9, you gain one additional Discipline rank of your choice: a new Discipline, or a rank in one you already have. Class-favored Disciplines, the ones your class gave you at creation, are always available. Cross-class Disciplines may require narrative justification or story events. Want your Blade to pick up Fire? Make it a story. Find a mentor. Touch a primordial flame. Earn it.

=== Magic Items

Magic items may grant temporary Disciplines while attuned. A _Blade of the Last Ember_ grants Fire rank 1 while you stay attuned to it. Break attunement and the power goes with it. These items are treasures, and the DA should make you work for them (see @sec-chapter-magic-items)

#pagebreak()

== Disciplines as Prerequisites

Abilities, talents, and spells require specific Disciplines before you can learn them. No Disciplines, no purchase. It's that simple. Skills are the one exception, they have no Discipline prerequisites at all (@sec-chapter-skills)

#figure(
  align(center)[#table(
    columns: (34.15%, 35.37%, 30.49%),
    align: (auto, auto, auto,),
    table.header([Card], [Disciplines Required], [Level Gate],),
    [Brimstone Burst], [2 Fire], [Level 3],
    [Beast Tongue], [1 Animal], [Level 1],
  )],
  kind: table,
  numbering: none,
  outlined: false,
)

=== The Wildcard Rank

One class holds a wildcard. The Odd's wildcard rank stands in for any Discipline when buying a card, and the player chooses which Discipline it stands in for each time. It has three limits. It satisfies a requirement of one rank, so it can never supply a second rank of a Discipline the hero already holds. It satisfies one requirement at a time. And it never advances: no progression pick can raise it, so it stays at rank 1 for the whole career.

== The One-Card Law

Every card is bought once, at one tier, for one price, and it never changes. The three tiers are *Novice*, *Adept*, and *Master*, and each tier is a separate card with its own name, its own level gate, and its own flat price. There is no ladder to climb and no upgrade to pay for. The card's tier sets the level you need (Novice 1, Adept 3, Master 7). The Disciplines printed on the card are a separate gate: hold those ranks and you can buy it. Skills use the same three tiers but gate nothing (@sec-chapter-skills)

=== Card Costs (Flat)

Cards cost Development Points at a flat rate regardless of class:

#figure(
  align(center)[#table(
    columns: (20%, 30%, 50%),
    align: (auto, auto, auto,),
    table.header([Tier], [Card DP Cost], [Level Gate],),
    [*Novice*], [2 DP], [Level 1],
    [*Adept*], [4 DP], [Level 3],
    [*Master*], [8 DP], [Level 7],
  )],
  kind: table,
  numbering: none,
  outlined: false,
)

=== Discipline Rank Costs (Per Class)

Each class pays a different price for each Discipline rank depending on how aligned that Discipline is with the class's identity. See @sec-chapter-classes for each class's Discipline cost table. The four cost structures are:

#figure(
  align(center)[#table(
    columns: (31.25%, 16.67%, 16.67%, 16.67%, 18.75%),
    align: (auto, auto, auto, auto, auto,),
    table.header([Cost Structure], [Rank 1], [Rank 2], [Rank 3], [Meaning],),
    [*Home*], [1 DP], [2 DP], [4 DP], [Favored: core to the class identity],
    [*Adjacent*], [2 DP], [4 DP], [8 DP], [Related but not core],
    [*Foreign*], [3 DP], [6 DP], [12 DP], [Unrelated to the class],
    [*Opposed*], [4 DP], [8 DP], [16 DP], [Out of class: antithetical to the class],
  )],
  kind: table,
  numbering: none,
  outlined: false,
)

=== Total Cost of a Card

The total cost of a card = its flat card DP cost + the sum of the Discipline rank costs from your class's structure for each required discipline.

#callout(type: "note", title: "Worked Total-Cost Example: Ember Lance vs Brimstone Burst", body: [
The flat card DP cost is only part of the price. You also pay rank costs for any required Disciplines you do not already possess.

*Ember Lance (Novice, 1 Fire):*
- *Protector* pays flat 2 DP + Fire rank 1 at Opposed cost (4 DP) = *6 DP total*.
- *Arcanist* already has Fire rank 1 from her class grant, so she pays the flat 2 DP only = *2 DP total*.

*Brimstone Burst (Adept, 2 Fire):*
- *Protector* (no existing Fire) pays flat 4 DP + Fire rank 1 at Opposed (4 DP) + Fire rank 2 at Opposed (8 DP) = *16 DP total*.
- *Arcanist* (already has Fire rank 1 from creation) pays flat 4 DP + Fire rank 2 at Home (2 DP) = *6 DP total*. If the Arcanist did not have Fire rank 1 yet, the total would be flat 4 + rank 1 (1 DP) + rank 2 (2 DP) = *7 DP*.

The same card can cost wildly different amounts depending on your class and what you already know. Build accordingly.
])

=== Discipline Requirements

A card's header names the Disciplines it needs: 1 Fire, 2 Melee, 2 Shields, and so on. Hold those ranks and meet the card's level gate, and you can buy it. A hero's maximum in any single Discipline is 3 ranks, so a card never asks for more than three.

Weapons, armor, and shields may list their own Discipline requirements as entry requirements: a Dagger needs 1 Melee, a Longsword 2 Melee, a Greatsword 2 Two-Handed, a Tower Shield 2 Shields, and Plate 3 Armor. See @sec-chapter-equipment and @sec-chapter-armor-shields A card's tier is separate from its equipment's entry requirement.

=== No-Prereq Basics

Some basic Novice cards (basic utility skills) have *no Discipline requirement* and cost only the flat card price (2 DP). These represent minor talents anyone can pick up: a knack for reading a room, a trick of sleight of hand, a steady hand on a wound. Cantrips are the one exception on price: they cost nothing, and every caster of a tradition knows the whole list (see @sec-chapter-arcane-spells and @sec-chapter-divine-spells). A card that prints no Discipline on its header needs none, whatever its tier. There are no shortcuts to real power.

#pagebreak()

== Damage Budget
#label("sec-damage-budget")

Every damaging spell, ability, and maneuver in _Heroes of Legend_ is built on a single table. This is the balance spine. Spells are the guide; everything else keys off them.

#figure(
  align(center)[#table(
    columns: (30%, 70%),
    align: (auto, auto,),
    table.header([Tier], [Damage (Weak / Standard / Strong)],),
    [*Novice*], [4/6/8],
    [*Adept*], [5/8/11],
    [*Master*], [7/10/14],
  )],
  kind: table,
  numbering: none,
  outlined: false,
)

#callout(type: "note", title: "How to Read the Budget", body: [
There is no damage roll. The outcome of your attack or casting roll (Weak, Standard, or Strong) determines your damage from the budget table. The hit roll is the damage roll.

The numbers are flat damage points. A Novice Ember Lance deals 4 damage on a Weak result, 6 on Standard, 8 on Strong. An Adept spell deals 5/8/11. These are flat numbers. No dice. If your homebrew spell or ability doesn't match this table, it's either too weak or too strong. The table is the law. The table is the balance.

See @sec-chapter-arcane-spells and @sec-chapter-divine-spells for the full spell lists. See @sec-chapter-classes for class abilities keyed to this budget.

Every damaging card states its expression in its damage line as either *Flat* or *Attribute-Scaled.*

*Flat* damage uses the budget row exactly as listed. Arrows, missile ammunition, thrown weapons, most spells, and all monsters use flat damage. No attribute is added.

*Attribute-Scaled* damage adds the card's stated attribute to a base value, minimum 1 damage. Novice cards use the Basic-card floor (1/2/3). Adept and Master cards use the budget row minus 3 (2/5/8 and 4/7/11), so a Novice card prints as "1/2/3 + Knowledge". Melee attacks add Brawn to their attack card's damage row. A talent from the substitution family can replace Brawn with another attribute when applicable. See @sec-chapter-talents-abilities. Missile weapons and ammunition are flat.

Weapons follow the cards, not their own curve: an attack ability card carries the damage (see the Equipment chapter for what each weapon unlocks). Melee attacks add Brawn; missile and thrown weapons are flat.
])

#pagebreak()

== Worked Example: Building a Fire Mage

Sera wants to burn the world. She's an Arcanist. Her class gives her 1 Fire and 1 Energy at creation. Her ancestry and culture grant additional Disciplines as well.

*Novice (Ember Lance):* Requires 1 Fire. Sera has 1 Fire. She qualifies immediately. Ember Lance costs 2 DP (flat card cost), and her Arcanist home cost for Fire rank 1 was already paid at creation. Ember Lance is hers on day one.

*Adept (Brimstone Burst):* Requires 2 Fire. Sera has 1 Fire, so she needs one more. At level 3 she takes Fire (now 2 Fire) and buys Brimstone Burst the moment the Adept gate opens. Most casters need several levels to reach Adept. Arcanists walk a shorter path to the flame.


Seven levels to master the fire. Disciplines got her to Master. No shortcuts. Just the path, walked one step at a time.

That's the Discipline system working as intended. Master spells should be achievable before your campaign's climax, but they should still mean something when you cast them. A Master card says "I built for this." When Sera's lance becomes a pillar of flame, everyone at the table knows she paid for it.
```
